name: The Law of Comparative Advantage
statement: Trade benefits both sides when each specializes in what it gives up the least to produce.
statementAccent: what it gives up the least to produce
meaning: The law of comparative advantage holds that a country or person gains by specialising in and exporting the goods it can produce at the lowest opportunity cost, importing the rest. What matters is not who is absolutely more efficient but who sacrifices the least of other goods to make a given one. Because relative costs differ, mutually beneficial trade is possible even when one party is worse, or better, at producing everything.
mechanism: The engine is opportunity cost. Each party concentrates on the good whose production costs it the least in terms of forgone alternatives, so total output rises, and trade at a price lying between the two parties' opportunity-cost ratios leaves both better off. The counterintuitive step is that this holds even when one country can produce everything more cheaply in absolute terms: as long as the ratio of its costs across goods differs from its partner's, specialisation and exchange still gain for both, which is why comparative, not absolute, cost governs.

examples.text: Ricardo's classic case: Portugal can make both cloth and wine with less labour than England, yet both gain if each specialises where its opportunity cost is lower and they trade.
A lawyer who types faster than her assistant still gains by leaving typing to the assistant, whose opportunity cost of typing is far lower, so both are better off.
Even a party that is worst at producing everything has a comparative advantage in whatever it is least bad at, and so a basis for beneficial trade.

variants.name: Absolute advantage
variants.text: Adam Smith's earlier idea that a nation should import whatever a foreigner makes more cheaply in absolute terms; comparative advantage's key advance is that trade gains even without any absolute edge.

variants.name: Gains from the terms of trade
variants.text: The insight that the size and split of the gains depend on where the trading price settles between the two parties' opportunity-cost ratios.

whyItMatters: It is the foundational intellectual case for free trade and specialisation and remains the main basis for most economists' support of open trade. Paul Samuelson cited it as the example of an economic truth that is both universally valid and not obvious, capturing why it is among the most important and counterintuitive results in the discipline, reshaping how nations think about who should produce what.

working.text: identify who sacrifices least of other goods to make a given one, since that, not absolute efficiency, sets who should specialise.
have each party concentrate on its lowest-opportunity-cost good and exchange, raising total output for both.
remember that a nation can gain overall while particular groups lose, so account for who bears the costs of trade.

limits: The classical model rests on simplifying assumptions: two countries and two goods, labour as the sole factor, labour mobile within but not across borders, constant returns to scale, full employment, and no transport costs. Real-world critiques note that a nation may gain in aggregate while specific groups lose, that the split of gains depends on the terms of trade, that dynamic and increasing returns escape the static model, and that international capital and labour mobility and global value chains complicate the picture. Its logical core is robust; its real-world application is contested.
misreadings: It is not the same as absolute advantage; the whole point is that trade can benefit both even when one party is more efficient at everything, so relative cost governs. It does not imply trade benefits everyone equally: the model shows mutual national gains, not that every individual or group within a country gains, and distributional losses are real. And a party that is worst at everything is not without a comparative advantage; it has one in whatever it is least bad at.
origin: Set out by David Ricardo in 'On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation' (1817), with the classic England-and-Portugal example, following an earlier formulation by Robert Torrens in 1815.

sources.text: Ricardo, On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation (1817), Ch. 7. — the England-Portugal example and the doctrine of comparative advantage.
